Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.14405v1 [cs.SE] 09 Oct 2026 SPROUT: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Software Engineering Mengyang Liu Weiming Wang Haixin Nan Yu Wu Peize Li Shihong Huang Xuning He Xue Jiang Yihong Dong October 9, 2026 SPROUT: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Software Engineering Mengyang Liu 1,2 Weiming Wang 1 Haixin Nan 3 Yu Wu 1 Peize Li 4 Shihong Huang 1 Xuning He 1 Xue Jiang 5 Yihong Dong 1,🖂 1 Shanghai Jiao Tong University 2 Amazon 3 Nanjing University 4 King’s College London 5 Peking University ABSTRACT Reinforcement learning (RL) has driven substantial progress in coding agents by relying on verified successful trajectories as learning signals. However, such trajectories are scarce in long-horizon software engineering tasks, where a minor error can invalidate the entire rollout. Repeatedly restarting from the initial state is commonly used yet inefficient, and resetting only the context with working directory misses state changes such as installed dependencies. Therefore, branching from intermediate steps to preserve earlier progress requires restoring both the agent context and execution environments. In this paper, we present SPROUT ( S na P shot-based R oll OUT ), an agentic RL rollout framework that scales long-horizon coding tasks by resuming and branching from intermediate states. Specifically, SPROUT was built on top of a lightweight infrastructure that checkpoints both the filesystem and the agent context after each assistant turn. A verifier-guided backtracking policy then selects where to resume a failed attempt and how to proceed. Extensive experiments on long-horizon coding tasks show that SPROUT achieves up to 23.6% improvement over pass@k across various LLMs, while using 32 32 – 52 % 52\% of their tokens. For RL training of Qwen3.8-27B, SPROUT stably outperforms standard GRPO by 13.9 13.9 points on three long-horizon coding benchmarks while cutting the time per training step by 39.5 % 39.5\% . SPROUT thus makes RL on long-horizon coding tasks both more effective and cheaper to scale. Code / Project Page Correspondence: dongyh@sjtu.edu.cn 0 0 footnotetext: Work done during research internships at RISE-X Lab, School of Computer Science, Shanghai Jiao Tong University. 0 0 footnotetext: Work conducted outside of the authors’ roles at Amazon. 0 0 footnotetext: 🖂: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Coding agents are becoming capable of completing increasingly long tasks in real software environments, such as resolving issues in large repositories ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024a ; Huang et al., 2026a ) . For such tasks, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the de facto training paradigm ( Shao et al., 2024a ; He et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2026 ) : the agent attempts a task in an executable environment, a verifier such as the task’s test suite checks the final result, and the policy is updated from these outcomes. Such training is especially expensive on long-horizon tasks. A single attempt may read a large, unfamiliar codebase, install dependencies, build artifacts, and run test suites, and it can take hours to finish. The longer the task, the harder it is to learn from. The verifier reward is usually binary, so an attempt receives credit only if its final solution passes. Over a long attempt, one wrong decision anywhere, such as an incorrect patch after hours of correct setup, is enough to make the reward zero, and successful attempts become rare as the horizon grows. In group-relative methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024a ) , a task whose attempts all fail has zero advantage for every attempt and contributes no gradient. The expensive rollouts spent on the hardest tasks thus produce no learning signal, even when most of their steps were correct. Two strategies are commonly used to obtain more positive signal. The first samples more attempts per task ( Brown et al., 2024b ; Li et al., 2022 ) , which multiplies an already high cost: every new attempt redoes its exploration and setup from scratch and can repeat the same mistake. The second branches from intermediate steps of earlier attempts. In a coding environment, this requires three things. The restored environment must match the agent’s context at the branch point, including the files the agent edited, the packages it installed, and the artifacts it built anywhere in the system. Checkpoints must be cheap enough to take at every step, since any step may turn out to be the right place to branch. The branch point itself must also be chosen well. Existing methods miss at least one of these requirements. Tree search and reflection methods ( Yao et al., 2023a ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ) , as well as CBPO ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , branch only within the conversation. Among RL methods that restore sandbox states, Shepherd ( Yu et al., 2026 ) versions only the agent’s workspace, BPO ( He et al., 2026a ) snapshots containers only at a few selected steps, and both rely on layered container snapshots with hard limits on depth. Full virtual machine snapshots are complete but must store guest memory at every step, making the storage requirement unacceptable on long horizon tasks. To choose branch points, BPO uses policy entropy without consulting the verifier, and Shepherd delegates the choice to a stronger external model. Their RL experiments focused on tasks normally take 8 - 25 steps, leaving long horizon unexplored. Figure 1: SPROUT: branch from checkpoints instead of restarting. Resuming a failed rollout from the step where it went wrong beats resampling it from scratch, at inference time and in RL. (a) DeepSWE, four models: SPROUT beats Pass@4 on every model while spending 48–68% fewer tokens; Shepherd and entropy-based branching do not. (b) RL with Qwen3.8-27B: training on SPROUT rollouts improves over GRPO by 7–25 pp on three mainstream agentic benchmarks. Each RL step is 40% faster and cheaper than sampling from the beginning. Figure 2: SPROUT reuses failed rollouts for efficient exploration. (a) Independent rollouts repeat costly prefixes. (b) Guided by verifier feedback, the same agent policy resumes from paired context and VM checkpoints to explore new continuations. In this paper, we present SPROUT ( S na P shot-based R oll OUT ), an agentic RL rollout framework that scales long-horizon coding tasks by resuming and branching from intermediate states. Sprout is composed of three components: 1) a restorable execution layer runs each attempt in a microVM ( Agache et al., 2020 ) and take a snapshot of its filesystem incrementally after every assistant turn, pairing each checkpoint with the matching agent context. 2) a verifier-guided backtracking policy decides where to branch (Figure 3 ): the actor itself reviews failed trajectories with the verifier’s feedback, chooses where to resume, and proposes the first action of the new continuation, so the recovered trajectories do not import knowledge from a stronger model. 3) a GRPO-based training procedure learns from the branched rollouts and distills the guidance used during search into the base policy. We evaluate SPROUT on various mainstream long-horizon agentic coding benchmarks, i.e., DeepSWE, Terminal-Bench 2.1, and SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard. Compared with a single attempt per task, SPROUT raises the resolve rate on DeepSWE from 72.3 % 72.3\% to 98.2 % 98.2\% with Kimi K3, from 46.9 % 46.9\% to 82.3 % 82.3\% with Claude Sonnet 5, and from 42.5 % 42.5\% to 85.8 % 85.8\% with GPT 5.6 Luna, exceeding four independent attempts while using 32 32 – 52 % 52\% of their tokens. For RL, we train Qwen3.8-27B with SPROUT on a subset of SWE-bench Rebench v2. Relative to the base model, training raises the resolve rate from 62.7 % 62.7\% to 84.3 % 84.3\% on SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard, from 37.2 % 37.2\% to 40.7 % 40.7\% on DeepSWE, and from 49.4 % 49.4\% to 64.0 % 64.0\% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, ahead of standard GRPO on the same tasks ( 74.5 % 74.5\% , 33.6 % 33.6\% , and 39.3 % 39.3\% ) while cutting the 39.5% of the time per training step. 2 Related Work Long-Horizon Coding Agents. Coding agents solve software engineering tasks by interleaving reasoning with tool calls in interactive environments ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Dong et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Frameworks such as Mini-SWE-agent ( Yang et al., 2024b ) , OpenHands ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , OpenCollab ( Hsu et al., 2026 ) , and Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2025 ) let them navigate repositories, edit code, and validate changes through execution, and benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified ( OpenAI, 2024 ) , SWE-bench Pro ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , DeepSWE ( Huang et al., 2026b ) , and Terminal-Bench 2.1 ( Merrill et al., 2026 ) evaluate them on increasingly long-horizon tasks. A single attempt can span tens to hundreds of tool calls and fail on a single error, after which it is usually discarded and resampled from scratch, redoing progress such as understanding the repository and localizing the root cause. SPROUT instead resumes failed attempts from intermediate states and reuses their prior progress. Tree Search and Backtracking. Repeated sampling increases task coverage but restarts every sample from the initial state ( Brown et al., 2024a ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Tree-search methods instead expand and backtrack over intermediate states ( Yao et al., 2023b ; Hao et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) , much as Go-Explore first returns to a visited state and then explores ( Ecoffet et al., 2021 ) , while reflection methods correct errors in later attempts using verbal or tool feedback ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Gou et al., 2024 ) . In software engineering, SWE-Search ( Antoniades et al., 2025 ) applies Monte Carlo tree search to issue resolution, and Shepherd ( Yu et al., 2026 ) delegates the choice of where to intervene over reversible traces to a stronger external model. Because agents edit files, install packages, and build artifacts, branching only within the conversation, as tree search and reflection methods do, leaves the environment inconsistent with the agent’s context, and Shepherd versions only the agent’s workspace. SPROUT restores the full filesystem together with the matching agent context and lets the actor itself, rather than a stronger model, use verifier feedback to choose where to branch and how to continue. Full scope : the restored environment covers the whole disk, not only a workspace. Per-step : every tool call of a long trajectory yields a restorable checkpoint. Compact : checkpoints keep incremental disk changes, snapshot is cheap enough for taking snapshot for each tool call. Failure-aware : branching uses verifier feedback on the failed attempt.
